questions.stem: Why is water from different sources treated by different methods?
options: Treatment methods depend only on the temperature of the water when collected
The impurities present depend on the source and on what the water is used for
Water from every source contains exactly the same impurities in different amounts
Only rainwater needs treatment, because river and bore water are already pure
questions.explanation: River water may carry suspended clay and microbes, bore water may be hard or saline, and sea water must be desalinated; drinking water also needs stricter treatment than water for irrigation. No natural source is reliably pure.

questions.stem: Which sequence is commonly used to remove suspended matter from river water?
options: Coagulation and flocculation, then sedimentation, then filtration
Filtration, then flocculation, then sedimentation and chlorination
Sedimentation, then reverse osmosis, then coagulation and filtration
Chlorination, then flocculation, then distillation and sedimentation
questions.explanation: Fine particles are first clumped together by coagulation and flocculation, the larger clumps settle out during sedimentation, and filtration removes what remains. Filtering first would quickly clog the filters with fine clay.

questions.stem: Why do fine clay particles stay suspended in water instead of settling?
options: Their surfaces are positively charged, so they are attracted to water's oxygen
They are less dense than water, so they float just below the surface
They dissolve in water to form ions, which cannot settle out of solution
Their surfaces are negatively charged, so the particles repel each other
questions.explanation: The silicate and aluminosilicate surfaces of clay particles carry negative charges, so like charges keep the tiny particles apart and they are too small to settle quickly. Clays are denser than water and do not dissolve.

questions.stem: How does adding a salt containing aluminium ions, Al³⁺, help remove suspended clay from water?
options: The aluminium ions oxidise the clay particles to gases that bubble out
The highly charged cations neutralise the negative charges, letting particles clump
The aluminium ions react with the clay to form a soluble compound that is then filtered out
The aluminium ions give the clay a negative charge so that it repels the water
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ ions are attracted to the negative clay surfaces and cancel their charge, so the particles no longer repel and can come together into larger flocs that settle. The clay is not dissolved or oxidised.

questions.stem: Why is a salt of Al³⁺ much more effective than an equal concentration of Na⁺ ions at flocculating negatively charged clay particles?
options: Each Al³⁺ carries three positive charges, neutralising more negative charge per ion
Al³⁺ ions are larger than Na⁺ ions, so they cover more of each clay particle's surface
Na⁺ ions carry a negative charge in water, so they are repelled by the clay
Al³⁺ ions have more electrons, so they form covalent bonds with the clay
questions.explanation: Highly charged cations are attracted more strongly to the negative surfaces and neutralise far more charge per ion, so fewer are needed. Al³⁺ is actually smaller than Na⁺, and Na⁺ is positive.

questions.stem: Long-chain cationic polymers are also added during water treatment. How do they help?
options: They dissolve the clay particles, so the water no longer looks cloudy
They react with dissolved salts, removing hardness from the water
Their positive groups attach to several clay particles, binding them into flocs
Their negative groups repel the clay particles so that they rise to the surface
questions.explanation: A long polymer chain with many positive sites can attach to several negatively charged particles at once, bridging them into larger flocs that settle and filter more easily. The polymer does not dissolve the clay or soften the water.

questions.stem: Which ions make water hard?
options: H⁺ and OH⁻
Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺
Na⁺ and K⁺
Cl⁻ and SO₄²⁻
questions.explanation: Hard water contains high concentrations of calcium and magnesium ions. Sodium and potassium salts are soluble and do not form scum with soap.

questions.stem: Which two problems are caused by hard water?
options: The water becomes strongly acidic, and it dissolves plastic pipes
Soap forms scum and lathers poorly, and scale builds up in kettles and pipes
Soap dissolves far too quickly, and the water rapidly corrodes copper hot water pipes
The water tastes salty, and it cannot be heated above about 80 °C
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ form insoluble salts with soap anions (scum), wasting soap, and on heating, carbonate scale deposits in kettles, hot water systems and pipes.

questions.stem: In a water softener, a zeolite holding Na⁺ ions is used. What happens as hard water passes through it?
options: Na⁺ ions on the zeolite react with Ca²⁺ ions to form solid calcium metal
The zeolite releases Ca²⁺ ions into the water in exchange for Na⁺ ions
The zeolite filters out water molecules and lets the Ca²⁺ ions through
Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions are held on the zeolite and Na⁺ ions are released
questions.explanation: Zeolites are aluminosilicates with a negatively charged framework that holds cations. Doubly charged Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ are held more strongly than Na⁺, so they replace it on the zeolite and Na⁺ passes into the softened water.

questions.stem: A zeolite softener exchanges Na⁺ for Ca²⁺. How many Na⁺ ions are released for each Ca²⁺ ion taken up?
options: Three
Four
Two
One
questions.explanation: Charge must balance on the zeolite: one Ca²⁺ ion takes the place of two Na⁺ ions. This is written Na₂Z(s) + Ca²⁺(aq) ⇌ CaZ(s) + 2Na⁺(aq).

questions.stem: A used zeolite softener is regenerated by washing it with concentrated sodium chloride solution. Using Na₂Z(s) + Ca²⁺(aq) ⇌ CaZ(s) + 2Na⁺(aq), why does this work?
options: The high [Na⁺] shifts the equilibrium to the left, releasing Ca²⁺ from the zeolite
The high [Na⁺] shifts the equilibrium to the right, binding more Ca²⁺ to the zeolite
Chloride ions react with the zeolite framework and replace the Ca²⁺ ions
Sodium chloride dissolves the old zeolite so that a fresh layer can form
questions.explanation: Increasing the concentration of a product shifts the equilibrium in the direction that uses it up, so Na⁺ returns to the zeolite and Ca²⁺ is washed out. The chloride ions are spectators.

questions.stem: In reverse osmosis, how is fresh water produced from saline water?
options: A membrane lets the ions pass through it while holding back the water molecules
Electric current pulls the ions out of the water through a charged membrane
Pressure forces water through a semi-permeable membrane, leaving the ions behind
Heat evaporates the water, which then condenses on a semi-permeable membrane
questions.explanation: Normally water moves by osmosis from the dilute side to the concentrated side. Applying a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure to the saline side pushes water the opposite way through the membrane, while dissolved ions are held back.

questions.stem: In reverse osmosis, why must the pressure applied to the saline water be greater than its osmotic pressure?
options: Otherwise the ions would block the pores and dissolve the membrane
Otherwise the salt would crystallise on the membrane surface at once
Otherwise the saline water would boil before it reached the membrane
Otherwise water would move from the fresh side into the saline side
questions.explanation: Without pressure, osmosis moves water towards the more concentrated solution. Only a pressure exceeding the osmotic pressure reverses this flow, driving water out of the saline side.

questions.stem: Which two methods are widely used for desalination?
options: Reverse osmosis and thermal distillation
Flocculation and sedimentation
Chlorination and filtration
Ion exchange and fermentation
questions.explanation: Desalination removes dissolved salts from sea or brackish water, by forcing water through a membrane or by evaporating and condensing it. Flocculation and filtration remove suspended particles but not dissolved salts.

questions.stem: How does thermal distillation produce fresh water from sea water?
options: Sea water is heated until the dissolved salts evaporate and are collected
Sea water is frozen, and crystals of salt are filtered out of the slurry
Sea water is boiled so the salts react with the steam to form a solid scale
Sea water is boiled and the steam is condensed, leaving the salts behind
questions.explanation: Water evaporates while the dissolved ions stay in the remaining brine, so the condensed vapour is fresh water. The salts are not volatile and do not evaporate. Boiling large volumes of water makes this method very energy-intensive.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of supplying a city's drinking water by desalination?
options: It adds large amounts of chlorine to the sea, killing marine life near the plant
It only works on river water, which must be piped long distances to the coast
It uses a lot of energy and produces concentrated brine that must be disposed of
It leaves the water too hard to drink unless zeolites are added to the plant
questions.explanation: Pumping water at high pressure through membranes, or boiling it, needs much energy, which can add greenhouse emissions, and the salty brine returned to the sea can harm marine life. Plants are also costly to build and run.

questions.stem: Which substances are used as oxidising agents to disinfect water?
options: Sodium chloride, sodium hydroxide and carbon dioxide
Nitrates, phosphates and potassium salts
Chlorine, hypochlorous acid and hypochlorites
Calcium carbonate, zeolites and aluminium salts
questions.explanation: Chlorine and the hypochlorous acid and hypochlorite ions it forms oxidise and kill microorganisms. Aluminium salts are flocculants and zeolites soften water; neither disinfects.

questions.stem: Chlorine reacts with water: Cl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCl(aq) + HOCl(aq). Which species formed is the main disinfecting agent?
options: Hydrogen ions, H⁺
Hypochlorous acid, HOCl
Hydrochloric acid, HCl
Chloride ions, Cl⁻
questions.explanation: Hypochlorous acid is the strong oxidising agent that kills microorganisms. HCl ionises to H⁺ and Cl⁻; chloride ions are not oxidising agents.

questions.stem: Cl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCl(aq) + HOCl(aq). Why is acid never added to a strong solution of chlorine or hypochlorite bleach?
options: Extra H⁺ shifts the equilibrium to the left, releasing toxic chlorine gas
Extra H⁺ shifts the equilibrium to the right, releasing toxic hydrogen gas
Extra H⁺ removes all of the HOCl, so the water boils as it is neutralised
Extra H⁺ shifts the equilibrium to the right, forming solid chlorine
questions.explanation: HCl is a product, so adding H⁺ increases the product concentration and the equilibrium shifts left, forming Cl₂, which escapes as a toxic gas. No hydrogen gas forms, and chlorine is a gas at room temperature, not a solid.

questions.stem: Pool water is chlorinated with sodium hypochlorite. Using OCl⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) ⇌ HOCl(aq), why is disinfection less effective if the pH rises well above 8?
options: More H⁺ ions shift the equilibrium right, so less OCl⁻ is present
Fewer H⁺ ions shift the equilibrium right, so more Cl₂ gas forms
More OH⁻ ions react with OCl⁻ to form a hypochlorite precipitate
Fewer H⁺ ions shift the equilibrium left, so less HOCl is present
questions.explanation: At high pH the H⁺ concentration is low, so the equilibrium lies to the left and most of the chlorine is present as hypochlorite ions, which disinfect much less effectively than HOCl. Pools are therefore kept close to neutral.

questions.stem: Why must plant nutrients in soil be in soluble form?
options: Soluble nutrients are heavier, so they sink to the level of the roots
Only soluble nutrients can be absorbed through the leaves when it rains
Plants absorb nutrients through their roots as ions dissolved in soil water
Plants absorb nutrients as solid particles that pass straight into the roots
questions.explanation: Roots take up nutrients as ions from the soil water, so nutrients locked in insoluble compounds are not available. Solid particles cannot pass into root cells.

questions.stem: Which three elements are the major nutrients that plants need from the soil?
options: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
Calcium, magnesium and sulfur
Iron, copper and zinc
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
questions.explanation: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (N, P and K) are the major nutrients supplied by most fertilisers. Plants get carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water, and iron, copper and zinc are needed only in tiny amounts.

questions.stem: Which natural process returns nitrogen from dead plants and animals to the soil?
options: Lightning, which breaks down dead matter into nitrogen gas and water
Photosynthesis, which converts dead matter directly into nitrate ions
Evaporation, which leaves nitrogen behind as dead matter dries out
Decay by decomposers, releasing ammonium ions that bacteria convert to nitrate
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down proteins in dead organisms and wastes to ammonium, and nitrifying bacteria oxidise it to nitrate, which plants absorb. Lightning fixes atmospheric nitrogen; it does not break down dead matter.

questions.stem: How does lightning add nitrogen to soil?
options: It splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, which combine with soil nitrogen
It burns organic matter in the soil, releasing ammonium ions as ash
It converts nitrate ions in the soil into nitrogen gas, which the plants then absorb
It makes N₂ and O₂ form NO, which becomes nitric acid and reaches soil as nitrate
questions.explanation: The very high temperature of lightning makes nitrogen and oxygen combine to form NO, which is oxidised to NO₂, dissolves in rain as nitric acid and enters the soil as nitrate ions. Plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly.

questions.stem: How do legumes such as clover and lupins add nitrogen to soil?
options: They convert phosphate ions in the soil into nitrate ions in their roots
Bacteria in their root nodules convert nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds
Their leaves absorb nitrate ions from the air and release them into the soil
Their roots release nitrogen gas, which reacts with oxygen in the soil
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria living in legume root nodules convert atmospheric N₂ into ammonium compounds that the plant uses; when the plant decays, this nitrogen enriches the soil.

questions.stem: Why do many farm soils need fertilisers although nutrients are recycled naturally?
options: Crops can only absorb nutrients from fertilisers, not from natural sources
Harvested crops remove nutrients that would otherwise return when plants decay
Fertilisers are needed to make insoluble nutrients in the soil dissolve in rain
Natural recycling stops completely once a field has been ploughed
questions.explanation: When crops are taken away, the nutrients they absorbed leave the field and are not returned by decay, so they must be replaced. Many soils are also naturally low in nutrients such as phosphorus.

questions.stem: Which fertiliser ions are most easily leached from soil into waterways, and why?
options: Nitrate ions, NO₃⁻, which are not held by the negative soil particles
Potassium ions, K⁺, which bind tightly to the negative soil particles
Ammonium ions, NH₄⁺, which are repelled by the negative soil particles
Calcium ions, Ca²⁺, which form insoluble salts with the soil silicates
questions.explanation: Soil silicate and aluminosilicate surfaces are negative, so they hold cations such as K⁺ and NH₄⁺ but not anions. Nitrate salts are all soluble, so nitrate washes out readily with rain or irrigation water.

questions.stem: Excess fertiliser washes into a lake, and weeks later fish die. Which sequence explains this?
options: Algae grow rapidly, die, and bacteria decomposing them use up dissolved oxygen
Nitrate ions poison the fish directly, and the dead fish then feed the algae
Phosphate ions react with dissolved oxygen, forming a layer of solid phosphate
Fertiliser raises the water temperature so that oxygen boils out of the lake
questions.explanation: Leached nitrogen and phosphorus cause algal blooms (eutrophication). When the algae die, aerobic bacteria decompose them and consume dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate. Algal mats also block light from water plants.

questions.stem: Which substances are important components of rocks and soils?
options: Silicon dioxide, silicates and aluminosilicates
Sodium chloride, nitrates and phosphates
Calcium carbonate, ammonia and urea
Hydrocarbons, alcohols and esters
questions.explanation: Most rock-forming minerals and clays are silicates and aluminosilicates, along with silicon dioxide (quartz). Nitrates and chlorides are very soluble and are only minor components of soils.

questions.stem: What is the formula of the anion in the silicate mineral Mg₂SiO₄?
options: SiO₄²⁻
Si₂O₄⁴⁻
SiO₂²⁻
SiO₄⁴⁻
questions.explanation: Two Mg²⁺ ions carry a total charge of +4, so the anion must be SiO₄ with a 4− charge. Check: Si (+4) plus four O (−8) gives −4.

questions.stem: What is the formula of the anion in the aluminosilicate mineral KAlSi₃O₈?
options: AlSi₃O₈²⁻
Si₃O₈⁻
AlSi₃O₈³⁻
AlSi₃O₈⁻
questions.explanation: One K⁺ means the anion has a charge of 1−. Check: Al (+3) + 3 Si (+12) + 8 O (−16) = −1. Aluminium stays in the anion, as it replaces silicon in the framework.

questions.stem: Anorthite is CaAl₂Si₂O₈. Using Si +4, Al +3 and O −2, what is the charge on its aluminosilicate anion?
questions.explanation: 2 Al (+6) + 2 Si (+8) + 8 O (−16) = −2, which balances the one Ca²⁺ ion. Each aluminium in place of a silicon adds one extra negative charge to the framework.

questions.stem: How do nutrient cations such as K⁺ and Ca²⁺ held on the surface of soil aluminosilicates become available to plants?
options: They become available only when the aluminosilicate dissolves completely in rain
They are released when bacteria convert them into nitrate ions in the soil
They are in equilibrium with cations in soil water and are released as those are used
They are absorbed by roots directly from the solid surface without entering water
questions.explanation: Adsorbed cations exchange with those in soil water. As roots take up cations from the water, the equilibrium shifts and more are released from the surfaces. Roots also release H⁺, which displaces adsorbed cations.

questions.stem: Root hairs release H⁺ ions into the soil around them. How does this help the plant take up nutrients?
options: H⁺ ions attach to anions such as nitrate, which makes them insoluble
H⁺ ions displace nutrient cations from soil particles into the soil water
H⁺ ions react with nitrogen gas in the soil to form ammonium ions
H⁺ ions dissolve the roots' cell walls so nutrients can flow straight in
questions.explanation: The H⁺ ions exchange onto the negatively charged surfaces of silicate and aluminosilicate particles, releasing cations such as K⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ into the soil water, where the roots can absorb them.

questions.stem: Why does a soil become less fertile if it becomes strongly acidic?
options: High [H⁺] binds nutrient cations more firmly to soil particles so none are released
High [H⁺] reacts with silicates to form nitrogen gas, which escapes from the soil
High [H⁺] converts the nutrient cations into anions, which roots cannot absorb
High [H⁺] displaces nutrient cations from soil particles, and they are leached away
questions.explanation: With a high concentration of H⁺ in the soil water, the exchange equilibrium shifts so H⁺ occupies the surface sites and nutrient cations are released into the water, where rain can wash them away. The soil's store of nutrients is depleted.

questions.stem: Irrigation with salty water raises the Na⁺ concentration in a soil. Why does this lower the soil's nutrient value?
options: Na⁺ forms a covalent coating over soil particles that stops water entering the soil
Na⁺ reacts with nitrate ions to form nitrogen gas, which escapes from the soil
Na⁺ is a major nutrient, so plants absorb it instead of nitrogen and phosphorus
Na⁺ replaces nutrient cations such as K⁺ and Ca²⁺ on soil particles, and they are leached
questions.explanation: A high Na⁺ concentration shifts the cation-exchange equilibrium so sodium occupies the surface sites, releasing nutrient cations into the soil water to be washed away. Sodium is not one of the major plant nutrients.
